cards.title: Machines around us
body: Many things you use at home and at work are **machines**.
A farmer uses an **axe** to cut wood. A worker uses a **wheelbarrow** to carry heavy loads. A tailor uses **scissors** to cut cloth.

cards.title: Simple machine
body: A **simple machine** is any device that helps us to do work **more easily and quickly**.
The axe, wheelbarrow and scissors are simple machines.

cards.title: Three ways machines help
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Force multiplier
states.text: Most machines are **force multipliers**. A **small** force overcomes a **large** force, but the small force must move a **long distance**.

states.label: Speed multiplier
states.text: Some machines are **speed and distance multipliers**. They increase the speed and distance of the movement.

states.label: Change direction
states.text: Many machines **change the direction** of the force. Here neither the force nor the distance changes.

cards.title: Summary: machines
body: A machine can **transfer** a force, **multiply** a force, **change the direction** of a force, or multiply **speed and distance**.

cards.q: Which one is NOT a simple machine?
cards.why: A bicycle is made of many machines together. The others are simple machines.

cards.title: Effort and load
body: The force **you** put on a machine is the **effort (E)**.
The force the **machine** puts out is the **load (L)**. The load is also the weight of the object to be lifted or moved.
In all machines, an effort at one place overcomes a load at another place.

cards.title: A crowbar
body: Tap the dots: effort, fulcrum and load.

cards.title: Mechanical advantage
body: **Mechanical advantage (M.A)** = load ÷ effort.
It shows how many times a machine **multiplies** the effort.
It is a ratio of two forces, so it has **no units**.

cards.title: Bigger, equal or smaller than 1
body: A machine can have M.A **greater than 1**, **equal to 1**, or **less than 1**.

cards.title: Worked example 1: find M.A
cards.problem: An effort of 200 N moves a load of 800 N in a wheelbarrow. Find the mechanical advantage.

steps.text: Given: E = 200 N, L = 800 N.

cards.title: Worked example 2: find the load
cards.problem: A boy pushes a bottle opener with 50 N. Its M.A is 3. What force does it put on the bottle cap?

steps.text: Given: E = 50 N, M.A = 3. Required: load.

cards.title: Worked example 3: find the effort
cards.problem: A machine has M.A = 5. What effort lifts a load of 300 N?

steps.text: Given: L = 300 N, M.A = 5. Required: effort.

cards.title: Memory trick: the M.A triangle
body: Draw a triangle: **L** on top, **M.A × E** below.
Cover what you want: L = M.A × E, M.A = L ÷ E, E = L ÷ M.A.

cards.q: A machine overcomes a load of 50 N with an effort of 10 N. Its M.A is:
What is the M.A of a machine that only changes the direction of the effort?
cards.why: The force does not change, so load = effort and M.A = 1.

cards.title: Six simple machines
body: There are **six types**: lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and pulley. Most machines are **combinations** of these.

cards.title: Memory trick: six machines
body: **Lazy In Winter, Sam Wants Pancakes.**

cards.title: Lever
body: A **lever** is a bar or rod that turns about a point.
The point it turns on is the **pivot** or **fulcrum (F)**.
The force on the lever is the **effort (E)**; the force it exerts is the **load (L)**.

cards.title: Levers every day
body: A **spoon** opens the lid of a tin. The lid moves **up** when you push the spoon **down**: the lever also changes direction.
A **claw hammer** pulls out a nail. A smaller force overcomes a greater force.

cards.title: The broom (Activity 1.4)
body: A pupil sweeps with a **broom**. She uses it as a lever.
Her hands move a **short** distance; the end of the broom moves a **long** distance. The broom is not a force multiplier; it multiplies distance.

cards.title: Three classes of levers
body: All levers have three parts: **fulcrum, load and effort**.
Levers are put in **three classes** by where the fulcrum is, compared with the effort and the load.

cards.title: Which part is in the middle?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: First class
states.text: **First-class lever (E-F-L)**: the **fulcrum** is between the effort and the load. Examples: **see-saw**, **crowbar**, **claw hammer**.

states.label: Second class
states.text: **Second-class lever (E-L-F)**: the **load** is between the effort and the fulcrum. Examples: **wheelbarrow**, **paper cutter**, **bottle opener**.

states.label: Third class
states.text: **Third-class lever (F-E-L)**: the **effort** is between the fulcrum and the load. Examples: **shovel**, **fishing rod**, **sugar tongs**.

cards.title: Memory trick: 1-2-3 = F-L-E
body: Say **F-L-E** (like "flea") for classes 1, 2, 3: the letter tells you what is in the **middle**.

cards.title: Inclined plane
body: Activity 1.5. Move the slider.

states.label: Lift straight up
states.text: Lifting straight up needs **more effort**, but the object moves a **short** distance.

states.label: Use a plank
states.text: Pulling along the plank needs **less effort**, but the object moves a **longer** distance.

cards.title: Inclined plane
body: An **inclined plane** is a flat, **sloped** surface, such as a plank of wood or metal.

cards.title: Wedge
body: Activity 1.6: the boy splits a log. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Wedges
body: A **wedge** is an inclined plane with **one or two sloping sides**.
Anything with a **sharp edge** is a wedge.
Examples: a **knife**, a **nail**, an **axe**, a **needle**, the digging part of a **plough**.
Wedges **increase force**. The M.A of a wedge increases when it is **longer and thinner**.

cards.title: Screws
body: A **screw** is a rod with a **thread** that goes both **up and round** the rod.
Screws **increase the force**: a small force on a screwdriver pushes the screw hard into wood.
Uses: to **fasten** things to wood, metal, glass and plastic, and to **make holes**.

cards.title: A screw is a rolled-up ramp

steps.text: Activity 1.7: cut a paper triangle. Colour the long side red. It slopes like a **ramp** (inclined plane).
Roll it round a pencil. The red line goes **up and round**, like the thread of a screw.
A **car jack** is a screw. A small force on the handle turns the screw and **lifts a car**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Wheel and axle
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Wheel and axle
body: A **wheel and axle** is two circles: a **wheel** and an **axle**. The axle has a **smaller radius**.
They are fixed together and **turn together**.
A **doorknob**: the knob is the wheel, the rod through the door is the axle. The big knob makes your force **larger**.
It lets a **smaller effort** overcome a **greater force**.

cards.title: Pulleys
body: A **pulley** is a **wheel with a groove** in its edge. A rope or chain runs round the groove.
Pull the rope, the wheel turns and the load moves.
There are two main kinds: **fixed** and **movable** pulleys.

cards.title: Fixed or movable?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Fixed pulley
states.text: A **fixed pulley** is fixed to a wall or support; it does not move. It does **not** change the force or distance, only the **direction**. **M.A = 1**. Used on a **flagpole** and to lift bricks and cement.

states.label: Movable pulley
states.text: A **movable pulley** is joined to the load and moves with it. It lets a **small force** lift the object, but the effort moves **twice as far** as the load. **M.A = 2**.

cards.title: Forces change motion
body: In Grade 6 you learned: a push or pull can **speed up**, **slow down** or **change the direction** of an object.

cards.title: Net force
body: Two or more forces can act at the same time.
The **combination of all the forces** on an object is the **net force**. It decides how the object moves.

cards.title: A box on a table

steps.text: The box is **at rest**. The forces on it balance: the net force is **zero**. It stays at rest.
You push it hard. Now there is a **net force**. It starts to move.
It slides and slowly **stops**. **Friction** between the box and the table acts on it.

body: Exercise 1.4. Tap Next.

cards.title: Newton's first law of motion
body: If there is **no net force** on an object:
it **stays at rest**, or
it **keeps moving** in a **straight line** at **constant speed**.

cards.title: Two parts of the law
body: a) An object **at rest** stays at rest if and only if the net force is **zero**.
b) A **moving** object keeps moving straight at **constant speed** only if the net force is **zero**.

cards.title: Isaac Newton
body: In **1665** Sir **Isaac Newton** began to relate forces to motion.
He said things do **not start or stop by themselves**: a net force must act on them.

cards.title: Nail near a magnet (Activity 1.11)
body: You, the magnet and gravity all pull on a nail, but it stays **at rest**.
The forces **balance** each other, so the net force is zero.

cards.q: A book sliding across a table slows down because:

options.A: you must push to keep anything moving
options.B: friction between the book and the table acts on it

cards.why: A net force (friction) slows the book. With no net force it would keep moving.

lessons.title: Effect of Force on Living Things

cards.title: Blood
body: **Blood** is a red liquid that flows through an animal's body.
The human body has about **4 to 6 litres** of blood.

cards.title: Two pumping forces

steps.text: The heart **contracts** and exerts a force. The **first** pumping force pushes blood to the **lungs** to get oxygen.
The blood returns from the lungs to the heart.
The **second** pumping force pushes blood from the heart to **all parts of the body**.
Blood moves round the body because of the **force** of the heart.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Seeds and seedlings

steps.text: **Pea and bean** plants keep their seeds in **pods** (a covering for seeds).
When the pods dry, they **crack and split open**. The seeds **shoot out with a force** and land far away.
A seed has a tiny plant asleep inside. With **water, heat and good soil** it wakes up. A **root** grows down and a **shoot** comes out of the soil. The shoot comes out because of **force**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Force in living things
body: The **heart** exerts a force to pump blood.
**Pods** of pea and bean shoot out seeds with a force.
A **shoot** pushes up out of the soil with a force.

cards.q: How much blood is in the human body?
cards.why: The book says about 4 to 6 litres.

units.title: Classification of Matter
units.intro: This unit is about elements, metals and nonmetals, mixtures, compounds and chemical reactions, and how to tell them apart.

u2mag.title: Separating a mixture with a magnet

cards.title: What is an element?
body: Doors and windows are made of iron, wood or aluminium. Electric wires are made of copper.
Iron, copper, aluminium, sulphur and carbon are **elements**.

cards.title: Element
body: An **element** is the **simplest** kind of substance.
It **cannot** be divided into simpler substances by **chemical means**.

cards.title: Examples
body: **Oxygen** is an element: it cannot be broken down.
**Water is not** an element: it is made of oxygen and hydrogen.
About **92** elements occur in nature. Everything is made of combinations of them.

cards.title: Chemical symbols
body: Tap each element.

cards.title: What is a chemical symbol?
body: Each element has a **chemical symbol**: a short way to write its name.
It has **one or two letters** from the **English or Latin** name.
Example: iron is **Fe**, mercury is **Hg**.

cards.title: Metals and nonmetals
body: Elements are grouped as **metals** and **nonmetals** by their properties.
About **80 %** of elements are metals.
Metals: gold, silver, iron, aluminium, copper, zinc, tin, mercury.
Nonmetals: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, sulphur, chlorine.

cards.title: Testing a sample (Activity 2.3)
body: Clip each sample into a circuit with a bulb. Move the slider.

states.label: Metal
states.text: With a **metal** such as copper, the **bulb lights**: an electric current passes.

states.label: Nonmetal
states.text: With a **nonmetal** such as sulphur or charcoal, the bulb does **not** light.

cards.title: Six properties of metals
body: Tap each one.

cards.title: Metals and nonmetals compared
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Sonorous
states.text: Metals are **sonorous**: they **ring** when hit. That is why bells are metal. Nonmetals do not ring.

states.label: Luster
states.text: Metals often have a **shiny** surface. This shine is called **luster**. Nonmetals are not shiny.

states.label: Malleable
states.text: Metals are **malleable**: they can be hammered into thin **sheets**. Nonmetals **break** when hit.

states.label: Ductile
states.text: Metals are **ductile**: they can be drawn out into long shapes. Copper makes **wires**; aluminium makes window frames.

states.label: Heat
states.text: Metals are good **conductors of heat**. Pots and frying pans are metal. Nonmetals are **poor** heat conductors.

states.label: Electricity
states.text: Metals are good **conductors of electricity**. Wires are metal (usually **copper**). Nonmetals usually do not conduct.

cards.title: Memory trick: six metal properties
body: **Shiny, Sings, Malleable, Ductile, Heat, Electricity** – think of a shiny **bell** on a copper **wire**.

cards.title: Gold
body: **Gold** is the **most malleable** metal.

cards.q: Which one is NOT an element?
cards.why: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.

cards.q: Why is copper used for electric wires?

options.A: It is a good conductor of electricity and ductile

cards.why: Copper conducts electricity well and can be drawn into wires.

cards.title: Mixture
body: A **mixture** is made of **two or more substances**.
They can be separated by **physical means**.

cards.title: Iron and sulphur (Activity 2.4)

steps.text: Mix iron filings and powdered sulphur. With a hand lens you still see **both**. It is a **mixture**.
Bring a **magnet** near. The iron filings are **attracted** because iron is magnetic. The sulphur stays.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Separating mixtures
body: The parts of a mixture can be separated by physical means:
**hand-picking**, using a **magnet**, **dissolving** and **boiling**.
**Soil** is a mixture: you can see dark and light grains.

cards.title: Two types of mixtures
body: Activity 2.5. Move the slider.

states.label: Heterogeneous
states.text: **Heterogeneous** mixtures: you **can see** the different substances. Examples: **muddy water**, **salad**, **sand and salt**.

states.label: Homogeneous
states.text: **Homogeneous** mixtures: you **cannot see** the different substances, even with a hand lens. Examples: **air**, **sea water**, **vinegar**, **mineral water**, **soft drinks**, **sugar in water**.

cards.title: Memory trick: hetero or homo?
body: **Hetero = you can tell the parts apart. Homo = it looks all the same.**

cards.title: Summary: mixtures
body: A mixture can be separated into its parts (**components**) by physical means.
In a homogeneous mixture the substances are spread **evenly**.

cards.q: Which one is NOT a mixture?
cards.why: Iron is an element.

cards.q: How can you separate sand and iron filings?
cards.why: The magnet attracts the iron filings, not the sand.

cards.title: Iron and sulphur heated (Activity 2.6)

steps.text: Mix iron filings and sulphur in a **crucible** on a **tripod** over a burner.
Heat gently for about **ten minutes**, cool and grind. You **cannot** see separate iron and sulphur, and a magnet **cannot** separate them. A **new substance** has formed.

body: Tap Next. Your teacher does the heating.

cards.title: Compound
body: A **compound** is made of **two or more elements** combined **chemically**.
It **cannot** be separated by physical means. You need **chemical means**.

cards.title: Common compounds
body: Figure 2.9: **salt**, **pure water** and **sugar** are compounds.

cards.title: New properties
body: A compound has its **own properties**, different from its elements.
**Water** is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Water is a **liquid**, but hydrogen and oxygen are **gases**.

cards.title: Burning paper (Activity 2.7)

steps.text: Look at a piece of paper.
Hold it with tongs in a candle flame. It **burns**.
Black **ash** is left. It is **not** like the paper: a **new substance** formed.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Chemical reaction
body: A **chemical reaction** (chemical change) is a change in which substances turn into **new substances**.
**Reactants**: the substances that react. **Products**: the new substances.

cards.title: Chemical equations
body: A **chemical equation** is a short way of writing a reaction. Reactants on the **left**, products on the **right**. Move the slider.

states.label: A + B → AB
states.text: "**+**" on the reactant side means **combines**. The **arrow** points to the products and means **forms**.

states.label: Carbon
states.text: Carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide. **Reactants**: carbon and oxygen. **Product**: carbon dioxide.

states.label: Magnesium
states.text: Activity 2.8: magnesium burns with a bright flame. Magnesium + oxygen → **magnesium oxide** (white powdery ash).

states.label: Kerosene
states.text: Review question: kerosene burns in air (oxygen). Kerosene + oxygen → **carbon dioxide + water vapour**.

cards.title: Everyday reactions
body: Cooking food, milk going **sour**, **photosynthesis**, burning wood or fuel, and **rusting** of iron are chemical reactions.
Some are **useful**, like photosynthesis. Some cause **problems**, like rusting.

cards.q: A mixture of powdered iron and sulphur is heated. What forms?
cards.why: The elements combine chemically to form a compound.

cards.q: Sulphur burns in air to form sulphur dioxide. The product is:
cards.why: Sulphur + oxygen → sulphur dioxide. The new substance is the product.

A mixture keeps the properties of its parts.

cards.title: Work in everyday life and in science
body: In everyday life, **work** means any physical or mental activity.
In **science**, work has a different meaning.

cards.title: Work
body: **Work** is done when a **force** moves an object in the **same direction** as the force.
Two things must happen: 1. a force acts; 2. the object moves in the direction of the force.

cards.title: Examples
body: You do work when you **lift** your school bag, **write** with a pen or **push** a trolley.

cards.title: Work or no work? (Activity 3.1)
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Heavy box
states.text: You push a heavy box but it does **not move**. You feel tired, but scientifically **no work** is done.

states.label: Lift a basket
states.text: You lift a waste-basket **up**. The force and the motion are in the **same direction**: **work is done**.

states.label: Carry it forward
states.text: You carry the basket forward. Your force is **up** but the basket moves **forward**. They are **not** in the same direction.

cards.title: More work
body: The work done depends on the **force** and the **distance**.
More work is done when **more force** is used, or the object moves a **greater distance**.

cards.title: Work formula
body: **Work done = force × distance** (W = F × S)
Unit: the **joule (J)**, named after James Prescott Joule.
1 J = 1 N × 1 m = 1 Nm

cards.title: Worked example 1: find the work
cards.problem: A painter lifts a can of paint with a force of 40 N through 2 m. How much work does he do?

steps.text: Given: F = 40 N, S = 2 m.

steps.text: Given: W = 100 J, S = 5 m.

steps.text: Given: F = 150 N, W = 600 J.

body: Cover the one you want: W = F × S, F = W ÷ S, S = W ÷ F.

cards.title: Energy
body: **Energy** is the **ability to do work**.
Without energy no work can be done.
The unit of energy is the **joule (J)**, the same as work.

cards.title: Examples
body: Water behind a **dam** and a **moving car** can do work because they have energy.

cards.title: Sources of energy
body: The **sun** is the **main** source of energy.
Food, petrol and coal are also sources.
Your arm gets energy to throw a ball from the **food** you eat.

cards.title: Renewable or non-renewable?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Renewable
states.text: **Renewable** sources do not finish after use: **sunlight, wood, water, wind**. Wood is renewable because we can **plant trees**.

states.label: Non-renewable
states.text: **Non-renewable** sources finish when we use them continuously: **coal, kerosene, diesel, petrol**. Use them **wisely** to avoid an **energy crisis**.

cards.title: Forms of energy
body: Figure 3.3. Tap each one.

cards.title: Mechanical energy
body: **Mechanical energy** comes from the position, condition or movement of an object.
It has two kinds: **kinetic** and **potential** energy.

cards.title: Kinetic and potential
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Kinetic
states.text: **Kinetic energy** is energy of **motion**. All moving things have it: wind, running water, a rolling ball. A still object has **no** kinetic energy.

states.label: Potential: height
states.text: **Potential energy** is **stored** energy because of position or condition. The **highest** brick has the **most** potential energy (Activity 3.3).

states.label: Potential: stretch
states.text: A **stretched rubber band** and **water in a dam** also store potential energy.

cards.title: Memory trick: K and P
body: **K**inetic = **K**eeps moving. **P**otential = **P**ut up high or **P**ulled tight.

cards.title: Heat energy
body: We get **heat** from fire and from the sun.
Our **body** also produces heat energy.

cards.title: Steam can move things (Activity 3.4)
body: Boil water in a kettle. The **lid moves**.
Steam turns a paper **windmill**: heat energy can make things move.

cards.title: Kettle and windmill
body: Figure 3.7.

cards.title: Chemical energy
body: Food, coal, wood and cooking gas contain **chemical energy**.
It is a **stored** form of energy. A candle flame comes from chemical energy stored in the **wax**.

cards.title: Light energy
body: The sun gives **heat and light** to the earth. Energy from the sun is **solar energy**.
Other light sources: burning oil, a **kerosene lamp**, **solar panels**.

cards.title: Electrical and sound energy
body: **Batteries** and **power stations** produce electrical energy. In Eritrea, most comes from **Hirgigo Power Station**.
**Sound** is made by **vibrations**: strings, car engines, drums, singing.

cards.title: Hydroelectric energy

steps.text: Water stored in a **dam** has **potential energy**.
The water falls onto **turbines**.
The turbines **rotate fast**.
The turbines turn **generators**, which produce **electricity**. This is **hydroelectric energy**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Wind energy
body: Wind energy can turn a **windmill**. Windmills are used to draw **water from wells**.
The Ministry of Energy and Mines works to use wind energy.

cards.title: Changes of energy
body: One form of energy can **change** into another form.

cards.title: A falling brick

steps.text: A brick held up high and at rest has **potential energy** but **no kinetic** energy.
Let it fall. Its potential energy **changes into kinetic** energy.
Near the ground it has the most kinetic energy.

body: Tap Next. Watch the bars.

cards.title: Photosynthesis
body: Green plants change **sunlight** into **chemical energy** stored as food. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Torch bulb (Activity 3.5)
body: The dry cell has **chemical energy**. It changes to **electrical** energy, then the bulb gives **light** (and heat).

cards.title: In a power station

steps.text: Fuel burns: **chemical** energy → **heat** energy.
Heat changes water in a boiler into **steam**.
The **kinetic energy** of the steam turns a **turbine**.
The turbine turns a **generator**. Kinetic energy → **electrical** energy.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Law of conservation of energy
body: **Energy is never created or destroyed.**
It only changes from one form to another. The total energy in the universe stays the same.

cards.title: Conserving energy
body: We **conserve** energy by using it **carefully and wisely**, without wasting it.

cards.title: Power in everyday life
body: People say someone has **power** when they are strong or have authority.
In **science**, power is **how quickly work is done**.

states.text: Berhe lifts it in **20 s**. They do the **same work**, but Ali is **faster**, so Ali is **more powerful**.

cards.title: Power formula
body: **Power = work done ÷ time taken** (P = W ÷ t)
Unit: the **watt (W)**, named after James Watt.

cards.title: Bigger engines
body: A **large engine** is more powerful than a small one: it does more work in the same time.

cards.title: Changes around living things
body: Living things are stimulated by many **changes** in their environment.
Some changes are **helpful** and some are **harmful**.

cards.title: What can stimulate a living thing?
body: Important factors: light, water, chemicals, gravity, heat and other living organisms. Tap each one.

cards.title: Key words
body: A **stimulus** is a change that makes an organism react. (Plural: **stimuli**.)
A **response** is the reaction to a stimulus.
**Sensitivity** is the ability to react or respond to stimuli.

cards.title: Why respond?
body: The **survival** of an organism depends on its ability to respond to stimuli.
All the responses an organism makes are its **behaviour**.

cards.title: Who controls behaviour?
body: In **higher animals**, the **nervous system** and the **endocrine system** control behaviour.
The endocrine system is a system of **glands**. They make chemicals that control body processes.
**Plants** and **simple animals** have no nervous or endocrine system. Their behaviour is controlled by **tropism**.

cards.title: How plants respond
body: Plants have **no sense organs**, no nervous system and no effectors.
They respond by changing the **rate** and **direction** of their **growth**.
This takes a **longer time** than animal responses.

cards.title: Two kinds of growth movement
body: 1. **Nastic movement**
2. **Tropism**

cards.title: Nastic movement (Figure 4.1)
body: Nastic movement does **not** depend on the **direction** of the stimulus. Move the slider.

states.label: Open
states.text: Normal leaves are **open**.

states.label: Touched
states.text: Lightly touch the plant: some leaves **close**. Direction does not matter.

states.label: Sunrise
states.text: Some flowers **open after sunrise**. This is also nastic movement.

cards.title: Tropism
body: **Tropism** is a growth movement **toward** or **away from** a stimulus.
Its direction depends on the **direction** the stimulus comes from.
**Positive** tropism: toward the stimulus. **Negative** tropism: away from it.

cards.title: Positive and negative phototropism
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Positive
states.text: A young seedling grows **toward** a light source: **positive phototropism**.

states.label: Negative
states.text: Roots grow **away from** light: **negative phototropism**.

cards.title: Memory trick: the name tells the stimulus
body: Tropisms are named after the stimulus.

steps.text: An **upright** pot: the stem grows **up**.
Lay a pot **on its side** in a dark cupboard.

cards.title: Why are tropisms slow?
body: Plants have **no locomotion** (they cannot move from place to place).
So their parts **grow** toward or away from a stimulus.
Leaves turn toward sunlight. Roots grow away from light but **toward moisture** in the soil.

cards.title: How animals respond
body: A change is detected by **receptors**.
Receptors pass the message to a **coordinator**.
The coordinator sends a message to **effectors**, which produce the **response**.

cards.title: The mechanism of sensitivity (Figure 4.5)

steps.text: **Stimulus**: a change in the internal or external environment.
**Receptor**: a cell, tissue or organ that receives the stimulus.
**Coordinator**: the **brain** or **spinal cord** organises a response for the body's needs.
**Effector**: a **muscle** or **gland** that produces the response.
**Response**: the reaction of the body to the stimulus.

cards.title: A reflex step by step

steps.text: **Stimulus**: the hand touches a **hot** pan.
**Receptors** in the skin detect the heat.
A message goes to the **coordinator** (spinal cord).
A message goes to the **effectors**: the arm **muscles**.
**Response**: the hand pulls away, very fast!

cards.title: Try it (Activity 4.4)
body: You feel an **itch** on your elbow and you scratch it.
Stimulus: the itch. Response: scratching.
Receptor: the skin. Coordinator: the brain. Effectors: the hand and arm muscles.

cards.title: Who can respond to both?

This is because they have a **nervous system** and an **endocrine system**. Humans have both.

cards.title: Harmful things inside the body
body: Substances are always exchanged between the cells and their surroundings.
If **harmful chemicals** or **germs** get in, the body responds in different ways, for example **vomiting** or **fever**.

units.title: Introduction to Agriculture
units.intro: This unit is about farming: soil, fertilizers, farm tools, crops, pests, livestock and mixed farming.

sub soil: brownish, rich in minerals
parent rock: the rock the soil forms from
rake: preparing seed-beds, collecting old plants

top soil: dark, rich in humus
sub soil: brownish, rich in minerals

cards.title: Agriculture
body: **Agriculture** uses **climate, water and soil** to produce **plants and animals** for human needs.

cards.title: More than crops
body: Agriculture is not only crops.
It also produces **food** (dairy products, poultry, honey) and materials for **clothing** and **shelter**.
It also deals with **distributing** farm products to the community.

cards.title: What does agriculture study? (Figure 5.1)
body: Tap each bubble.

cards.title: Agriculture in Eritrea
body: Our **basic needs** are food, clothing and shelter. Agriculture helps produce them.
About **85%** of Eritrea's people depend directly on agriculture.
So the Eritrean economy is **based on agriculture**.

cards.title: Why agriculture is important
head: Agriculture…
rows: is the main source of food for people and animals
is a main source of jobs

cards.title: Memory trick: FRESH
body: Five reasons agriculture matters.

cards.title: Training farmers
body: Training helps farmers produce **more and better** food.
This improves their **living standard** and helps the **national economy**.

cards.title: Debesay's sick ox (Activity 5.2)
body: Debesay's ox is sick. He thinks an “evil eye” caused it.
Traditional treatments (leaves, an egg broken on its back) do not help.
He asks **Zahra**, a veterinary worker, for help.

cards.title: How Zahra found the answer

steps.text: **Problem**: the ox is very sick.
Zahra **asks** questions and **observes**: slippery mucus, eats little, less active.
She makes a **guess**: maybe Rinderpest.
She **tests** a blood sample in the laboratory.
**Result**: the virus disease Rinderpest. She gives the right medicine.

body: Tap Next. Zahra used a scientific method.

cards.title: Primitive and modern agriculture
body: **Primitive** agriculture used soil, rain, and local plants and animals just as they were.
**Modern** agriculture uses the **scientific method** and **technology** to produce more.

cards.title: Agriculture is a science
body: Agriculture is a **science** because it uses the **scientific method** to solve problems.
It improves the **quality** and **amount** of farm products.

cards.title: Soil
body: **Soil** is the natural top covering of the earth's surface.
It **supports** plants and gives them **mineral nutrients** and **water**.

cards.title: How soil forms: weathering

steps.text: Start with a big **rock**.
Changes in **heat, water and wind** crack the rock. This is **weathering**.
The rock breaks into **small particles**: soil. Weathering is **very slow**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Other ways soil forms
body: The **decay** of dead plants and animals.
**Human activities**: construction, farming, war.

cards.title: Try it (Activity 5.3)
body: Rub two soft rocks together over paper.
Small particles fall: this is how rocks can become soil.

cards.title: Soil profile and texture
body: **Soil texture**: how fine or coarse the particles are.
**Soil profile**: a vertical section of soil showing its **layers**, from the top down to the parent rock.

cards.title: A typical soil profile (Figure 5.2)
body: Tap each layer.

cards.title: Memory trick: Top, Sub, Rock = T-S-R
body: From the top down: **T**ea, **S**ugar, **R**ock.

cards.title: What is in soil?
body: Soil has **minerals, water, air, humus** and **living organisms**. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Minerals and water
body: **Mineral particles** come from the parent rock. They are also called **mineral salts**.
They dissolve in water and plant roots absorb them.
The **water** in soil changes with wind and sunlight. It is usually around the mineral particles.

cards.title: Water in soil (Activity 5.4)
body: Weigh 100 g of garden soil. Dry it for a few days. Weigh it again.
The soil gets **lighter** because the **water** leaves it.

cards.title: Air in soil (Activity 5.5)

steps.text: Take 100 cm³ of dry soil and 100 cm³ of water.
Add the water to the soil and **shake**. Watch for bubbles.
Read the level and compare it with 200 cm³. The spaces between soil particles are usually filled with **air**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Why soil air matters
body: Bigger particles give bigger air spaces.
Soil air gives the gases for **respiration** of organisms in the soil.

cards.title: Humus and living things
body: **Humus** forms when the remains of plants and animals **decay**. It is at or near the surface.
It has important **nutrients** for plants.
Many organisms live in soil: rats, rabbits, beetles, ants, termites, **earthworms** and microscopic organisms. Some **decompose** remains.

cards.title: Three main kinds of soil
body: Soils differ in particle size, texture and colour.
By particle size and texture there are **sandy soil**, **loam soil** and **clay soil**.

cards.title: Look closely at the particles
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Sandy
states.text: **Sandy soil**: large particles, coarse texture, a **light** soil. Big spaces between grains.

states.label: Clay
states.text: **Clay soil**: very fine particles, a **heavy** soil. Only small spaces.

states.label: Loam
states.text: **Loam soil**: medium texture, a balanced mix of sand and clay, with humus.

cards.title: The funnel test (Activity 5.8)
body: Pour 50 cm³ of water into each funnel at the same time. Move the slider.

states.label: Sand
states.text: Drainage in sandy soil is **very fast**, so the most water comes through.

states.label: Loam
states.text: Drainage in loam is **very good**.

states.label: Clay
states.text: Drainage in clay is **poor**: clay holds water well.

states.label: Compare
states.text: Most water through: sand. Least: clay.

cards.q: Which soil is best for many plants?
cards.why: Loam has very good drainage and aeration and enough humus (p. 103).

cards.title: Fertile soil
body: A **fertile** soil has the essential minerals for healthy plant growth: **plant nutrients**.
It gives a **high yield** of crops.

cards.title: Five ways to improve soil fertility
head: Way
How it helps
rows: rest the land a year or more

cards.title: Memory trick: Clever Farmers Can Love Fields
body: Five ways to improve soil fertility.

cards.title: Controlling soil erosion
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Contour
states.text: **Contour ploughing**: furrows run **around** a slope. Water collects in them. This stops run-off and helps water sink in.

states.label: Terraces
states.text: **Terraces**: the land is cut into **wide, flat steps**. Water stays longer, erosion is controlled.

states.label: Strips
states.text: **Strip cropping**: crops in rows **across** the slope, with rows of **grass or gravel** between to slow run-off.

cards.title: Crop rotation and fallowing
body: The same crop every year removes the **same minerals**. So farmers **change** the crop year after year.
**Fallowing**: leave the land **unplanted** for a year or more. No crops use its minerals, so it regains fertility.

cards.title: Legumes add nitrates

steps.text: The air has **nitrogen gas**.
**Bacteria** in the roots of legumes (peas, beans, groundnuts, lentils) take it in.
They change it into useful **nitrates**, essential minerals for plants.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Fertilizer
body: A **fertilizer** is a substance added to the land to improve **soil fertility**.
Two types: **natural** and **artificial** (commercial).

cards.title: Natural fertilizers (manure)
head: Type
How it is made
rows: waste of farm animals is collected and left to decompose
farmers sow seeds, then plough and bury the green plants; they become humus

cards.title: Artificial fertilizers
body: They are made in **industries**.
The three essential ones: **nitrogen**, **phosphorus** and **potash** fertilizers.

cards.title: Memory trick: N-P-K
body: The three commercial fertilizers.

cards.title: What manure or fertilizer does
head: Benefit
rows: makes the soil easy to dig or plough

cards.title: Farm activities
body: Farmers clear the land, plough, add fertilizers, plant crops, control weeds and harvest.
They need tools for each activity.

cards.title: Farm tools (Figure 5.4)
body: Tap each tool.

cards.title: Simple farm tools (Table 5.1)
head: Tool
Use
rows: collecting and spreading crops, grass or manure
preparing seed-beds, collecting old plants and weeds
moving loose soil, fertilizers and grains

cards.title: Planning and clearing
body: Farmers should **plan** so they can use the land for many years.
First **clear** the land: cut trees and bushes, remove stones. Then **plough**, then plant.

cards.title: Why plough?
head: Advantage
rows: turns the soil so air moves in and out freely
allows proper drainage, so roots get enough water
buries weeds; they decay into humus

cards.title: Weeds and timing
body: **Weeds** compete with crops for nutrients, water, space and light.
Do not plough when the soil is **wet** or **too dry**: you get large lumps.
Many farmers start after the **first showers**.

cards.title: Pests and pesticides
body: **Pests** are animals that destroy crops in the field or in storage.
**Pesticides** are poisonous chemicals that control pests.
Pesticides are **dangerous** if not handled with care. Ask the Ministry of Agriculture or vendors how to use them.

cards.title: When pests attack
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Seedlings
states.text: **Armyworms** eat crops at the early **seedling** stage.

states.label: Grown crops
states.text: **Locusts** and **chaffer beetles** destroy large areas of grown crops.

states.label: Storage
states.text: **Rats** and **weevils** destroy the harvest in **storage**.

cards.title: Why food can be short
body: Most farmers use **traditional** ways: hand-hoeing or animal-drawn tools.
They depend on **rain**. Without enough rain, crops are poor and food is short.

cards.title: How to increase crop production
head: Way
rows: use the best seeds (high yield, suit the area, resist disease)
introduce irrigation (river or dam water by channels or pipes)
harvest on time and store safely

cards.q: Which is NOT a pest?
cards.why: Locusts, armyworms and rats are listed as pests (p. 110).

cards.title: Livestock
body: **Livestock** are animals kept on a farm for their **service** or as a source of **money**.
Examples: cattle, goats, sheep, poultry, bees, pigs, horses, donkeys, mules, camels.

cards.title: Why keep livestock?
head: Purpose
From
rows: meat, milk, milk products, eggs, honey

cards.title: Basic needs for livestock farming
head: Need
Meaning
rows: enough nutritious food for good products
mating selected male and female animals
clean shelter, fresh air, regular exercise

cards.title: Artificial insemination
body: A modern way to improve animals.
**Semen** from a selected male is put into the female's reproductive organ.
Only **trained people** do it.

cards.title: Mixed farming
body: **Mixed farming** is producing **crops and livestock** together.
Many Eritrean farmers practise it.

cards.title: Why mixed farming helps
body: Animals give **manure** for the land. The land gives **fresh grass** for animals.
The farmer must be ready for **both** jobs.

units.intro: This unit is about ecosystems, food chains and webs, biomes, and how communities change over time.

cards.title: Living things affect each other
body: Some organisms live **cooperatively**. Some get benefits at the **expense** of others.
Almost all organisms **compete** for things in short supply.

cards.title: Ecology
body: The **environment** is all the living and non-living things that affect an organism.
**Ecology** is the study of how organisms relate to **one another** and to their **environment**.

cards.title: Four key words
body: **Habitat**: the place where an organism lives.
**Population**: organisms of the **same species** in the same habitat at one time.
**Community**: all the living things that interact in a habitat.
**Ecosystem**: the communities plus their **non-living** environment.

cards.title: From one organism to an ecosystem

steps.text: One organism.
Many of the **same species** together: a **population**.
All the populations living together: a **community**.
The community **plus** the non-living environment: an **ecosystem**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Habitats
body: Examples: a pond, stream, field, garden soil, forest, leaf litter, rotting log, seashore, mountain top, tree bark, a small village.
A **river** is a habitat for fish, frogs, snakes and plants.

cards.title: A river ecosystem
body: Tap the dots. Which are living and which are non-living?

cards.title: Memory trick: H-P-C-E, small to big
body: **H**appy **P**eople **C**reate **E**cosystems.

cards.title: A self-contained unit
body: In an ecosystem, living things interact to get **all the substances** they need.

cards.title: Try it (Activity 6.1)
body: Walk around your school. Find small ecosystems: lawns, trees, cracks with plants, flower beds, ponds, drains.
List the animals and plants, where they live and how many (numerous or rare).

cards.q: Organisms of the same species in the same habitat at one time are a:
cards.why: Same species → population (p. 121).

cards.title: Two groups of factors
body: **Biological factors**: the **living** parts and their activities.
**Physical factors**: the **non-living** parts (light, water, oxygen, temperature, soil).

cards.title: Biological or physical?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Biological
states.text: Food, predators, diseases and **competition** for food, air, water, light and space. Human activities too.

states.label: Physical
states.text: Light, water, oxygen, temperature and soil. They decide **which organisms** can live in an area.

cards.title: Humans affect ecosystems
body: Cutting down many plants and releasing **harmful substances** harm ecosystems.
As a result **floods, droughts** and **pollution** happen more often.

cards.title: A stable community
body: An organism survives only if the right **mix** of biological and physical factors is present.
A **stable community** survives without change as long as the same conditions exist.

cards.q: Which is a PHYSICAL factor?
cards.why: Temperature is non-living (p. 124).

cards.title: Energy starts with the sun
body: All living things need **energy**. All the energy in an ecosystem comes from the **sun**.
Green plants change **light energy** into **chemical energy** in food by **photosynthesis**.
Plants use some energy and **store** the rest. Animals get it when they eat plants.

cards.title: Producers and consumers
body: **Producers**: green plants. They make food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
**Consumers**: animals and non-green plants. They cannot make food using sunlight.

cards.title: Memory trick: Herb, Carn, Omni
body: **Omni** means **all**: plants and animals.

cards.title: Decomposers
body: **Decomposers** break down dead plants and animals into **simple substances**.
Plants can use these substances **again and again**.

cards.title: How energy and matter move (Figure 6.2)

steps.text: The sun gives light to the **producers**.
Producers are **eaten by** consumers.
Producers and consumers **die**. **Decomposers** feed on them.
They **decay** into simple substances in the soil. Plants **absorb** them again.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Did you know?
body: Decomposition can take **many years**.
Without decomposers we would be surrounded by piles of ‘natural rubbish’!

cards.title: Respiration
body: **Respiration** is how living things get energy from food.
Food + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

cards.title: Food chain
body: A **food chain** is a series of organisms through which **energy** passes as **food**.
Arrows show the direction food (energy) moves.
A food chain **always starts with a green plant** or its products.

cards.title: Three food chains (Figure 6.3)
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Land
states.text: grass → grasshopper → lizard → snake

states.label: Water
states.text: tiny water plants → tadpole → fish

states.label: Farm
states.text: grass → sheep → man

cards.title: Make chains (Activity 6.3)
body: From the pictures: a lion eats a zebra; a zebra eats grass. So: **grass → zebra → lion**.
A locust eats grass; a mouse eats a locust: **grass → locust → mouse**.
A worm eats a leaf; a bird eats a worm: **leaf → worm → bird**.

cards.title: Food web
body: Each organism can be in **several** food chains.
Two or more **connected** food chains make a **food web**.

cards.title: A food web (Figure 6.5)
body: Follow the arrows. The mouse is eaten by the hawk **and** the fox.

cards.title: Chains inside the web
body: grass → rabbit → fox
grass → grasshopper → small bird → hawk
grass → mouse → hawk

cards.q: A food chain always starts with:

cards.title: Biome
body: A **biome** is a **large area** with the **same climate**.
It has many ecosystems and its own typical plants and animals.

cards.title: Kinds of biomes
body: Tap each branch.

cards.title: Land biomes
body: Most land biomes are named after their main **vegetation**.
This is because vegetation decides all the other living things there.
Major land biomes: tundra, coniferous forest, deciduous forest, tropical forest, grassland (savannah), desert.

cards.title: Water biomes
body: **Marine** (saltwater): seas, seashores, oceans. **Freshwater**: rivers, streams, ponds, lakes.
Water biomes are **more stable** than land: water is plentiful and the climate changes less.

cards.title: Memory trick: The Cat Did Try Getting Down
body: The six land biomes.

cards.title: Ecological succession
body: A community is **not permanent**. It changes slowly and in order.
**Ecological succession** is the continual **replacement** of one community by another.

cards.title: Where does it happen?
body: It happens when new communities colonise a **new area**.
Examples: a forest floor after a **fire**, an unused farm field, an unused demolished site.

cards.title: After a forest fire (Figure 6.7)

steps.text: **A.** Fire drives away mammals, flying insects and birds. It kills most plants.
**B.** Grass grows. It feeds **herbivores**. Carnivores come too.
**C.** Bushes and shrubs appear.
**D.** Trees slowly **replace** shrubs. Leaf-eating insects and fruit-eating birds come.
**E.** A full forest: the **climax community**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Climax community
body: The **final** community, in balance with living and non-living factors.
It is **stable** while conditions (like climate) stay the same. It supports many forms of life.

cards.title: What can disturb a stable ecosystem?
head: Changes
rows: loss of minerals in the soil

cards.title: Universe and solar system
body: The **universe** is space with stars, planets, moons and more.
The **solar system** is a small part of it: the **sun**, its planets, their moons and smaller bodies.
The **sun** is at the **centre**.

cards.title: Star, planet, moon
body: A **star** is a large body that makes its own **energy**: heat and light.
A **planet** moves around a star. The Earth is a planet.
A **moon** moves around a planet. The Earth has **one** moon.

cards.title: Why does the sun look so big?
body: The sun is a star. It is the **nearest** star to us.
Other stars look like twinkling points of light.
We cannot see them in the day: the sun's light is **brighter**.

cards.title: The planets in order (Figure 7.1)
body: The book lists **nine** planets, starting nearest the sun. Tap each one.

cards.title: Memory trick: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming Planets
body: The book's nine planets, in order from the sun.

cards.title: Orbits
body: Planets move round the sun in fixed paths called **orbits**.
The orbits are **not exactly circular**.

cards.title: Two orbits (Figure 7.2)
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Earth
states.text: The Earth moves round the **sun** in its orbit.

states.label: Moon
states.text: The **moon** moves round the **Earth**.

cards.title: Play the solar system (Activity 7.1)
body: One pupil holds a card saying SUN in the middle of the field.
Nine pupils walk around on nine circles: they are the **planets** on their **orbits**.

cards.q: The Earth is the ___ planet from the sun.
cards.why: Mercury, Venus, **Earth**: third.

cards.title: Two motions
body: The Earth is always moving.
It **rotates** (spins) and it **revolves** (goes round the sun).

cards.title: Rotation
body: The Earth spins around an imaginary line through the **North** and **South Poles**: the **axis of rotation**.
This spinning is **rotation**, like a spinning bottle top (Activity 7.2).

cards.title: The axis (Figure 7.5)
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Day and night
body: As the Earth rotates, **half** of it gets sunlight: **day**.
The other half gets no sunlight: **night**.
One full rotation takes **24 hours**. This is called a **day**.

cards.title: Day and night in Eritrea (Activity 7.3)

steps.text: A torch (the sun) shines on Eritrea on a globe: it is **day** there.
Turn the globe **half a turn** anticlockwise. Eritrea is on the dark side: **night**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Revolution
body: **Revolution** is the Earth moving **round the sun**.
One revolution takes **365¼ days**: one **year**.

cards.title: Seasons
body: The Earth's axis is **tilted** as it goes round the sun.
**Seasons** are caused by this **tilt**.
Seasons are parts of the year with their own kind of weather.

cards.title: Four seasons (Figure 7.9)
body: Summer, autumn, winter and spring. They happen in different months in different regions. Tap each.

cards.title: Rotation does not cause seasons
body: The rotation of the Earth has **no effect** on seasons.
The cycle of seasons repeats every year.

cards.title: Memory trick: Rotate = Rest of the day, Revolve = Round the year

letters.m: 365¼ days, a year, seasons (with the tilt)

body: Spin → day. Go round → year.

cards.q: How many revolutions old are you if you are 13?
cards.why: One revolution = one year.

cards.title: Gravitational force
body: All objects in the universe **attract** each other.
This force is **gravitational force** (force of gravity).

cards.title: What keeps things going round?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Ball
states.text: Swing a ball on a string (Activity 7.5). The **string** pulls it and keeps it in a circle.

states.label: Moon
states.text: Gravity between the **Earth** and **moon** holds the moon in its orbit.

cards.title: Planets and gravity
body: All stars, planets and moons attract each other.
Gravity makes all the planets **revolve round the sun** in their orbits.
All objects, large or small, have a pull of gravity.

lessons.title: Light Sources in the Solar System

cards.title: Two kinds of bodies
body: **Luminous** bodies make their **own light**: the sun and other stars.
**Non-luminous** bodies have no light of their own. They **reflect** light: moons and planets.

cards.title: Luminous or non-luminous?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Luminous
states.text: The sun and stars give out their own light.

states.label: Non-luminous
states.text: The moon and planets only reflect sunlight.

cards.title: Our main light source
body: The sun is the nearest star to the Earth.
It is the **main source of light** to the Earth.

cards.title: The moon shines by reflection
body: The side of the moon facing the sun is always **lit**. The other side is always **dark**.
We only see the part that reflects light.

cards.title: Phases of the moon
body: **Phases** are the changes in the moon's shape and size as we see it.
They depend on the moon's **position** relative to the sun and the Earth.

cards.title: A lunar month (Figures 7.12 – 7.13)

steps.text: **Day 0 – new moon.** The moon is **between** the Earth and sun. Its side facing us is dark: we see **no moon**.
**Day 7 – half moon.** Half of the side we see gets sunlight.
**Day 14 – full moon.** The **Earth** is between the moon and sun. We see a **bright disc**.
**Day 21 – half moon** again.
**Day 28 – new moon** again.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Lunar month
body: A **lunar month** is one full revolution of the moon round the Earth.
It is about **28 days**.

cards.title: Memory trick: 0-7-14-21-28
body: Add 7 each time.

units.intro: This unit is about electric charges, circuits, conductors, series and parallel circuits, magnets, compasses and electromagnets.

cards.title: Charges
body: All matter is made of **atoms**. Atoms have **protons**, **neutrons** and **electrons**.
Protons are **positive** (+). Electrons are **negative** (–).

cards.title: Inside an atom
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Rubbing moves electrons

steps.text: Rub a balloon on your hair.
**Electrons** move from your hair to the balloon. These charges do **not** flow on.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Electricity
body: **Electricity** is a **continuous flow of electrons**, for example through electric wires.

cards.title: Sources of electricity (Figure 8.1)
body: We make electricity from solar, chemical, heat and mechanical energy. Move the slider.

states.label: Battery
states.text: A **dry cell** (battery).

states.label: Sun
states.text: **Solar panels** use the sun.

states.label: Water
states.text: **Running and falling water** turns generators.

cards.title: Using electricity
body: At home: lamps, electric stoves, radios, televisions.
Also in factories, schools, hospitals, offices and shops.

cards.title: Dry cells
body: The end with **+** is the **positive** end. The end with **–** is the **negative** end.
When electricity flows along wires, there is an **electric current**.

cards.title: Circuits
body: An **electric circuit** is the path of an electric current.
**Closed** circuit: electricity goes from the source to the device and **back**.
**Open** circuit: there is a **gap**, so no electricity flows.

cards.title: Switch off, switch on (Figure 8.3)
body: A **switch** opens or closes a circuit. Move the slider.

states.label: Off
states.text: Switch **off**: a gap. **Open** circuit. The bulb is off.

states.label: On
states.text: Switch **on**: the gap closes. **Closed** circuit. The bulb lights.

cards.title: Circuit symbols (Figure 8.4)
body: A **circuit diagram** uses symbols. It is quick and easy to draw. Tap each symbol.

cards.title: Remember the cell symbol
body: In the cell symbol the **long thin** line is the **positive** end.
The **short thick** line is the negative end.

cards.title: Conductors and insulators
body: **Conductors** let electricity flow: **copper**, **silver**.
**Insulators** (non-conductors) do not: **plastics**, **wool**.

cards.title: Test a material (Activity 8.3)
body: Put a material between the crocodile clips. Move the slider.

states.label: Lights
states.text: The bulb **lights**: current flows. The material is a **conductor**.

states.label: No light
states.text: The bulb stays **off**: no current. The material is an **insulator**.

cards.title: Why plastic covers wires
body: Current flows in the metal inside a wire.
Plastic is an insulator, so it covers the wire.

cards.title: Battery and voltage
body: A **battery** is two or more cells connected together.
**Voltage** is the force that pushes electrons through a circuit. Unit: the **volt (V)**.
A dry cell may say **1.5 V**. A **voltmeter** measures voltage; connect it **across** a cell or bulb.

cards.title: Two ways to join cells
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Series
states.text: **Series**: the positive end of one cell joins the negative end of the next. Torches and toys use this.

states.label: Parallel
states.text: **Parallel**: the positives join together and the negatives join together.

cards.title: Memory trick: Series = Single file
body: Series bulbs stand in a queue. Parallel bulbs stand side by side.

cards.title: Bulbs in series and parallel (Activity 8.5)

steps.text: **Series**: bulbs one after another. **One path** for the current. They **share** the battery's voltage.
Take one bulb out: a **gap**. The only path is broken, so the other bulb goes **off**.
**Parallel**: bulbs side by side. **More than one path**. Each bulb gets the **same voltage**.
Take one bulb out: the other path still works. The other bulb stays **on**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Why houses use parallel circuits
body: Lamps and devices in houses are in **parallel**.
Each one works **on its own**. You can switch one lamp off without affecting the others.

cards.q: An electric current flows only in:
cards.why: A closed (complete) circuit has no gap (p. 161).

cards.title: Magnets
body: **Magnets** pull metal objects towards them. A magnet can be made of **iron**.
Shapes: **bar**, **horse-shoe** and **U-shaped**.

cards.title: Magnet shapes (Figure 8.16)
body: Tap each magnet.

cards.title: Magnetic or not?
body: **Magnetic** substances are attracted by a magnet.
**Non-magnetic** substances are not.

cards.title: Magnetic poles (Activity 8.7)

steps.text: Roll a magnet in paper clips. Most clips stick at the **ends**: the **poles**.
Hang the magnet. It always comes to rest pointing **north–south**.
Break a magnet: each piece has a **north** and a **south** pole.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Poles
body: The pull is **strongest** at the two ends: the **poles**.
Every magnet has a **north** pole and a **south** pole. Poles come in **pairs**.

cards.title: Push or pull? (Activity 8.8)
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Like poles
states.text: Two north poles or two south poles **repel** (push away).

states.label: Unlike poles
states.text: A north and a south pole **attract** (pull).

cards.title: Memory trick: Likes Repel, Opposites Attract
body: Same pushes away. Different pulls together.

cards.title: The compass (Figure 8.19, Activity 8.9)
body: A compass has a small magnet needle that is free to turn. Move the slider.

states.label: Alone
states.text: The needle always points **north–south**. People use it to find **directions**.

states.label: Near a magnet
states.text: A magnet near the compass **turns** the needle away from north–south.

states.label: Earth
states.text: The **Earth** acts like a big bar magnet. Its magnetic poles are near its geographic poles.

cards.title: Sailors and compasses
body: Sailors use compasses to find their way.
Before compasses, they used the **sun** or the **stars**.

cards.title: Make an electromagnet (Activity 8.10)

steps.text: Wind insulated wire about 50 times round an iron nail. Connect it to cells and a switch. Switch **off**.
Switch **on**: the nail becomes a magnet and picks up pins.
Switch **off**: the nail is no longer a magnet. The pins drop.

cards.title: Electromagnet
body: An **electromagnet** is a magnet made by an **electric current**.
It is a magnet **only** while current flows. It can be turned **on and off**.

cards.title: Uses of electromagnets
body: Collecting and separating **iron and steel** from other materials in factories.
Electric **motors**, electric **bells** and **loudspeakers**.

units.intro: This unit is about body changes at puberty, why early pregnancy is dangerous, and how to protect yourself from sexually transmitted diseases.

u9male.title: How sperm cells leave the body

cards.title: Puberty
body: Boys and girls grow at almost the **same rate** until about age **10**.
Between **11 and 18** the body changes from a child's to an adult's.
This stage is **puberty** (adolescence). Girls usually change **faster** than boys after 10.

cards.title: Growing up (Figures 9.1 – 9.2)
body: Changes can be **physical**, **functional** or **behavioural**. Move the slider.

states.label: Child
states.text: Until about 10, boys and girls grow at almost the same rate.

states.label: Puberty
states.text: From about 11 to 18 the body changes.

states.label: Adult
states.text: The body of an adult.

cards.title: Changes at puberty (Summary, p. 189)
head: Boys
Girls
rows: hair on face, chest, armpits and around the sex organs
hair in armpits and around the sex organs

cards.title: How girls develop
body: A girl is born with a vagina, a womb and two ovaries.
At puberty they **enlarge** and start to work. They make it possible to have babies.

cards.title: The female reproductive organs (Figure 9.3)
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Female organs and their jobs
head: Organ
Job
rows: carry the ovum to the womb; fertilization usually happens here
strong muscular wall; carries a baby until birth
the door of the womb; opens wide at birth

cards.title: Health
body: Girls should keep their bodies **clean**.
The book says circumcision of girls is **harmful** and an old tradition.

cards.title: Ova
body: A girl is born with thousands of immature ova.
At puberty, **one ovum** matures each month, from one ovary, then the other ovary the next month.

cards.title: The monthly cycle

steps.text: An **ovum** matures in an ovary.
It moves along the **fallopian tube** to the womb.
If it is **not fertilized**, it dies. There is no pregnancy.
The inner lining of the womb **breaks and bleeds**. Blood and the dead ovum come out: **menstruation**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Menstruation
body: **Menstruation** is the monthly bleeding. It is a **sign of maturity**.
It usually comes every **28 days** and lasts **4 – 5 days**. This is the **menstrual cycle**.
Some girls have irregular cycles (e.g. 21 or 35 days). It can be painful for some.

cards.title: During pregnancy
body: If the ovum is **fertilized**, there is pregnancy.
The womb lining does not break, so menstruation **stops** until the baby is born.

cards.title: How boys develop
body: A boy is born with a penis, two testes and a scrotum.
At puberty they **enlarge** and start to work.

cards.title: Male organs and their jobs
head: Organ
Job
rows: make millions of sperm cells from puberty
sac of skin that covers the testes
carry sperm from the testes to the penis
passes urine; the urethra opens here

cards.title: How sperm cells leave the body

steps.text: The **testes** make sperm cells.
**Sperm tubes** carry them towards the penis.
Glands add a fluid that keeps sperm alive. Sperm + fluid = **semen**.
Semen passes out through the **urethra**. This is **ejaculation**. It is **not harmful**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.q: Where are sperm cells produced?
cards.why: The testes produce sperm cells (p. 189).

cards.title: How pregnancy happens
body: At puberty, boys make **sperm cells** and girls make **egg cells**.
After sexual intercourse a sperm may **fertilize** an egg. Then a girl can become **pregnant**.
**Pregnancy** is the time from fertilization to birth.

cards.title: Children need grown-ups
body: For adults, having children is important and has social value.
It needs **maturity, readiness and money**.
Young people are **too young** to take this responsibility.

cards.title: Early pregnancy is dangerous
body: Early age pregnancy is **dangerous** and its consequences are very serious.
Avoid early sexual intercourse. Stay away from situations that arouse sexual feelings.

cards.title: The egg baby (Activity 9.5)

steps.text: Pretend an egg is your baby. Carry it everywhere for **one week**. Do not let it break, get too hot or too cold.
You looked after an egg for a week. A child needs care for **many years**, and much more than an egg!

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Abstinence
body: **Abstinence** means saying **no** to sexual activity before marriage.
At early ages it is the **best** way to prevent pregnancy.

cards.title: Ask yourself first (p. 191)
head: Question
rows: What is my future educational plan?
Do I need this at this age? Why?
How will it affect my health?
Who would help me raise a child?

cards.title: Contraceptives (for adults)
body: **Contraceptives** are methods or materials adults use to prevent unwanted pregnancy.
Examples in the book: **condoms**, **pills** and **injections**.
**None** of them prevents pregnancy 100%.

cards.title: How each method works (book)
head: Method
How it works
rows: stops sperm cells from reaching the egg
taken every day as a medical person instructs; stop the ovaries releasing an egg

cards.q: The best way for young people to prevent pregnancy is:
cards.why: The book says abstinence is the best method at early ages (p. 191).

cards.title: STDs
body: Some diseases pass from person to person through **sexual intercourse**.
They are **sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)**: e.g. gonorrhea, syphilis and AIDS.

cards.title: Three STDs
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Gonorrhea
states.text: Caused by a **bacterium**. Burning pain when urinating. Cured if treated properly; untreated it can cause **sterility**.

states.label: Syphilis
states.text: Caused by another **bacterium**. Painless spots and rashes. Cured if treated; untreated: sterility, paralysis, madness, even death.

states.label: AIDS
states.text: Caused by a **virus**, HIV. A killing disease. **No vaccine** and **no cure** so far.

cards.title: HIV and AIDS
body: **AIDS**: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome. **HIV**: Human Immuno-deficiency Virus.
HIV can infect **anyone**, whatever their age, sex, religion, colour, education or work.
Youth are more affected because they are sexually active.

cards.title: Signs of AIDS
body: Fast weight loss, fever, continuous diarrhoea, skin cancers, swollen glands, tiredness, continuous coughing, night sweats.

cards.title: Where HIV is found
body: In an infected person, HIV is in the **blood**, **semen**, **vaginal fluids** and **breast milk**.

cards.title: HIV is NOT spread by…
body: eating food with an infected person
mosquito or bed bug bites

units.title: Reproduction and Inheritance
units.intro: This unit is about asexual and sexual reproduction, pollination, and how genes pass traits from parents to offspring.

cards.title: Reproduction
body: **Reproduction** is how living things make new individuals like themselves.
It keeps a **species** going from generation to generation.
A **species** is a group of similar organisms that can breed to make fertile offspring.

cards.title: Asexual reproduction
body: New individuals come from **one parent** only. No sex cells are needed.
The young are the **same** as the parent and each other. It is **quick**.

cards.title: Five kinds of asexual reproduction
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Budding
states.text: A **bud** is a small outgrowth. Buds on a leaf or stem grow into new plants or branches.

states.label: Bulbs
states.text: A **bulb** is an underground bud with fleshy leaves full of food. Each onion bulb can grow into a new plant.

states.label: Tubers
states.text: A **tuber** is a swollen underground stem with stored food. New shoots grow from potato **eyes** (buds).

states.label: Runners
states.text: A **runner** grows along the ground and makes roots and a new plant some distance away.

states.label: Slips
states.text: A **slip** is a cut piece of stem. Planted in soil, it grows roots. Vines grow from slips.

cards.title: Memory trick: Big Bright Tomatoes Run Slowly

cards.title: Sexual reproduction
body: New individuals come from the **union of sex cells** (**gametes**).
Usually **two parents** of opposite sex are needed, after **sexual maturation**.

head: Cells

rows: growth and replacing old or dead cells

cards.title: Why offspring are different
body: Each offspring gets some features from the **male** parent and some from the **female** parent.
So they differ from each other and from their parents.

cards.title: Parts of a flower
body: The **pistil** has the stigma, style and ovary. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Pollination
body: **Pollination** is moving pollen from the **anther** to the **stigma**.
Wind, water, insects or birds carry pollen.

cards.title: Self or cross?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Self
states.text: **Self pollination**: pollen goes to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.

states.label: Cross
states.text: **Cross pollination**: pollen goes to a flower of the same species on a **different** plant.

cards.title: From pollen to seed (Figure 10.8)

steps.text: A pollen grain lands on the **stigma**.
A **pollen tube** grows down the **style**.
It carries the male gamete to an **ovule** in the ovary.
They join: **fertilization**. The **zygote** is in the ovule. Ovule → **seed**; ovary → **fruit**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Reproduction in animals
body: Mammals are born with their sex already determined.
Reproduction is not possible until **sexual maturation**.
**Mammals** feed their young with milk: cows, goats, donkeys, cats, sheep, camels.

cards.title: Sperm cell and ovum (Figures 10.9 – 10.10)
body: Both have a nucleus with **chromosomes**, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. Only the sperm has a tail. Tap the dots.

cards.title: From zygote to baby (Figure 10.11)

steps.text: A sperm fertilizes an ovum, usually in the **fallopian tube**. This makes a **zygote**: one cell.
The zygote divides into 2 cells, then 4, and so on.
It becomes a tiny ball of cells: an **embryo**.
The embryo gets food and oxygen through the **placenta**. By the **third month** organs like the heart form: a **fetus**.
The fetus grows into a **baby** ready to be born.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Inheritance and traits
body: A **trait** is a characteristic, e.g. hair colour, eye colour, height, skin colour, nose type.
**Inheritance** is how parents pass traits to their offspring.

cards.title: The nucleus
body: Every cell has a **nucleus**. It controls all the cell's activities.
It contains thread-like **chromosomes**. Their number is fixed for each organism.

cards.title: Pairs or singles?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Body cell
states.text: In a **body cell**, chromosomes are in **pairs**.

states.label: Sex cell
states.text: In a **sex cell**, chromosomes are **single**: half the number.

cards.title: Worked: body cell or sex cell?
cards.problem: A sperm cell has 12 chromosomes. How many does a skin cell of the same organism have?

steps.text: A sperm cell is a sex cell. A skin cell is a body cell.
A body cell has double the number of a sex cell.

cards.title: Genes
body: A chromosome carries many **genes**, the hereditary materials.
Genes are arranged like **beads on a necklace**.
An offspring gets **half** its chromosomes from each parent.

cards.title: Genes and traits (Figures 10.12 – 10.14)

steps.text: Genes are on chromosomes. In a body cell, chromosomes and genes are in **pairs**. **A pair of genes decides one trait**.
When a cell divides to make sex cells, the pair **separates**. So sex cells have **single** genes.
At fertilization a gene from the **father** pairs with a gene from the **mother**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Gene symbols
body: Use the **first letter** of a trait. One letter = one gene; two letters = a pair.
**T** = tall, **t** = short (the opposite). **TT** and **tt** are pairs.
**B** = black, **b** = white.

cards.q: Why are genes single in a sex cell?

options.B: the pairs separate during cell division

cards.title: Homozygous and heterozygous
body: **Homozygous**: a pair of the **same** genes, e.g. TT, tt, BB, bb.
**Heterozygous**: a pair of **different** genes, e.g. Tt, Bb.

cards.title: Dominant and recessive
body: In a heterozygous pair, only one gene's effect shows.
The gene that shows is **dominant** (capital letter). The hidden one is **recessive** (small letter).
**Tt** is **tall**, because T is dominant.

cards.title: Memory trick: Capital wins
body: A small letter shows only when it has a small partner: **tt**.

cards.title: Genetic cross
body: At fertilization, each gene from the male gamete **pairs** with a gene from the female gamete.
This is a **genetic cross**. It happens in all sexually reproducing plants and animals.

cards.title: Worked example: TT × tt

steps.text: Cross a homozygous **tall** plant (TT) with a homozygous **short** plant (tt).
Pollen grains carry **T**; egg cells carry **t**.
Fill the table: every box is **Tt** (4 combinations).
All offspring are **Tt** and look **tall**, because T is dominant.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Try it: Activity 10.8 (TT self pollinated)
cards.problem: A homozygous tall plant (TT) is self pollinated. What will the new plants look like?

steps.text: Both parents are TT. All gametes carry T.

steps.math: T \times T \rightarrow TT,\ TT,\ TT,\ TT

steps.text: All TT: all tall.

cards.title: Try it: Activity 10.9 (tt self pollinated)
cards.problem: A homozygous short plant (tt) is self pollinated. What will the new plants look like?

steps.text: All gametes carry t.

steps.math: t \times t \rightarrow tt,\ tt,\ tt,\ tt

steps.text: All tt: all short.

cards.title: Try it: Activity 10.10 (Bb × Bb)
cards.problem: A heterozygous brown-eyed man (Bb) and woman (Bb) have children. What eye colours are possible?

steps.text: Each parent makes gametes B or b.
BB and Bb look brown (B is dominant). bb shows the opposite colour.
So 3 of the 4 combinations are brown.

cards.answer: brown (3 of 4 boxes) or the opposite colour, bb (1 of 4)
